prompt: A manufacturer is rolling out a new ERP system across 3 plants over the next 12 months. Draft an implementation sequencing plan with named phases, owners, and the single biggest sequencing risk.
context: Plant A (largest, 400 employees, most complex custom workflows) is HQ and has the most engaged sponsor (COO). Plant B (150 employees) has the simplest processes and volunteered to go first in a stakeholder survey. Plant C (220 employees) has a plant manager who has publicly expressed skepticism about the project. The vendor recommends a "pilot then scale" approach; internal IT has capacity to support one plant's go-live at a time, with a mandatory 6-week stabilization period after each go-live before starting the next.

binaryCriteria.description: Recommends Plant B (simplest processes, willing stakeholders) as the first go-live/pilot site, not Plant A or Plant C.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if Plant A (largest/most complex) or Plant C (skeptical) is recommended to go first.

binaryCriteria.description: Explicitly addresses Plant C's skeptical plant manager with a change-management approach (e.g., using Plant B's proof points), rather than ignoring the stated skepticism.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if Plant C's skepticism is not mentioned or addressed in the sequencing rationale.

binaryCriteria.description: Identifies attempting concurrent go-lives across plants (violating the stated one-at-a-time IT capacity constraint) as the single biggest sequencing risk.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the plan proposes or fails to warn against running two plants' go-lives at the same time.

goldNotes: A strong plan sequences Plant B first as the pilot (simplest processes, most willing stakeholders — lowest risk to prove the model), followed by stabilization, then either Plant C or Plant A next. It should recommend Plant C before Plant A specifically to convert the skeptical plant manager using early proof points from the Plant B pilot (a change-management rationale), saving the largest/most complex site (Plant A) for last when the implementation team has the most experience — rather than naively sequencing by size or sponsor enthusiasm alone. Given the 6-week mandatory stabilization period after each go-live and 3 plants, the plan should show a realistic timeline (roughly go-live-stabilize-go-live-stabilize-go-live, easily consuming most of the 12 months when including pre-go-live prep) and name owners per phase (e.g., project sponsor, plant-level change lead). The single biggest sequencing risk to flag: attempting to run two plants' go-lives concurrently to save time, which the context explicitly states IT capacity does not support.
